title: Understanding llama.cpp, GGUF, and Local CPU Inference
author: Anurag Mohan

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges (Part 15)
In the previous part, I tried to connect a few confusing pieces together:

CUDA
PyTorch
vLLM
CPU inference
GPU inference
model routing
load balancers
edge inference
Agentic AI

That article helped me build a better layered mental model. At the bottom, there is hardware. Above that, there are compute runtimes. Above that, there are model execution frameworks. Above that, there are inference engines. Above that, there are routers, gateways, and agent systems. But after writing that, one question became more interesting to me:
How does local or CPU-friendly inference actually work?
That leads naturally to:

llama.cpp
GGUF
quantized models
local inference
CPU inference
This article is my attempt to understand that layer better.
Why talk about llama.cpp now?
So far, a lot of the inference series focused on large-scale serving concepts:

KV cache
batching
multi-GPU inference
distributed serving
request routing
GPU communication
prefill vs decode
continuous batching
PagedAttention
vLLM architecture
Those concepts are very important for production GPU inference. But inference is not only about massive GPU clusters. There is another important side:

Can we run useful models locally?
Can we run smaller models on CPUs?
Can we use quantized models efficiently?
Can we build simple private endpoints?
Can we experiment without always needing GPUs?
This is where llama.cpp becomes very interesting.
What is llama.cpp?
At a simple level:

llama.cpp
=
a lightweight inference runtime
for running LLMs efficiently
in C/C++
It became popular because it made local LLM inference much more practical. Instead of needing a large cloud GPU setup just to experiment, we can run smaller and quantized models on:

laptops
desktops
CPU servers
edge devices
small cloud instances
That does not mean it is only for CPUs. It can also use GPU acceleration depending on the hardware and backend. But the important point is:
llama.cpp made local and resource-conscious inference much more accessible.
How is llama.cpp different from vLLM?
This was one of the first things I wanted to clarify for myself. Both can run LLM inference. But they are optimized for different situations. A simple mental model:

vLLM
=
high-throughput serving engine
for many concurrent requests,
especially GPU-backed serving

llama.cpp
=
lightweight local / CPU-friendly / quantized inference runtime
for running models efficiently on commodity hardware
That is not a perfect definition, but it is useful. vLLM shines when we care about:

serving many users
continuous batching
PagedAttention
GPU utilization
distributed inference
production serving
llama.cpp shines when we care about:

local inference
small models
quantized models
simple deployment
CPU-friendly experiments
edge-style workloads
Are they competing tools?
Not exactly. I think it is better to see them as tools for different parts of the inference landscape. For example:

Large model
many concurrent users
GPU cluster
production endpoint
This sounds like a vLLM-style problem. But:

small model
local machine
quantized model
private experiment
CPU server
This sounds like a llama.cpp-style problem. So the question is not:
Which one is better?
The better question is:
Which runtime matches the workload?
Why is llama.cpp important for learning?
For me, llama.cpp is useful because it makes inference feel tangible. When learning only through diagrams, concepts can remain abstract. But when I can actually:

download a model
run a local server
send a prompt
measure latency
compare quantization formats
change CPU threads
observe tokens/sec
the concepts become more real. This is especially useful after writing so many conceptual articles. At some point, I want to move from:
understanding inference systems
to:
running inference systems
llama.cpp is a very good bridge for that.
What problem does llama.cpp solve?
The basic problem is:

How can we run LLMs efficiently
without always needing a huge GPU setup?

Large models are expensive to serve. They need memory. They need compute. They need optimized runtimes. But not every task needs the largest model. For many practical tasks, a smaller model may be good enough. Examples:

basic summarization
classification
simple chat
routing decisions
local assistant tasks
structured extraction
draft generation
If a small quantized model can solve the task, then running it locally or on CPU can be very attractive.
What makes CPU inference difficult?

CPUs are general-purpose processors. They are flexible, but they do not have the same massive parallel compute profile as GPUs. A GPU is built for large parallel tensor operations. A CPU is built for broader general-purpose workloads. So for LLM inference, CPUs usually face challenges like:

lower parallel compute
lower memory bandwidth compared to GPU HBM
slower token generation for larger models
limited throughput for high concurrency
So CPU inference is not magic. It is a tradeoff.
Then why use CPUs at all?
Because CPUs are everywhere. They are available in:

laptops
desktops
cloud VMs
enterprise servers
edge devices
developer machines

They are also simpler to access than GPUs in many cases. For learning and experimentation, that matters a lot. If I can run a small model quickly on CPU, I can test ideas without waiting for GPU capacity. For some workloads, CPU inference may also be cheaper or easier to operate. So the value is not:
CPU beats GPU
The value is:
CPU is useful for the right workload.
What changed to make CPU inference more practical?
A few things came together. First, smaller models became much better. Today, models in the range of:

1B
3B
7B
8B
can be useful for many tasks. Second, quantization became more practical. Third, tools like llama.cpp made it easier to run quantized models efficiently. So the question shifted from:
Can I run the biggest model?
to:

What is the smallest model
that can solve this task well enough?
That question is very important for real inference systems.
What is GGUF?
GGUF is a model file format commonly used with llama.cpp. A simple mental model:

GGUF
=
a packaged model file format
that llama.cpp can load and run
When downloading models for llama.cpp, we often see files like:

model.Q4_K_M.gguf
model.Q8_0.gguf
model.F16.gguf
These filenames usually tell us something about the quantization format. For example:
represent different ways the model weights are stored.
Why does the model file format matter?
Because running an LLM is not only about the model architecture. The runtime needs to load:

weights
metadata
tokenizer information
quantization details
architecture details

The file format helps package these things in a way the runtime understands. So when I use llama.cpp, I am usually not downloading a raw PyTorch checkpoint directly. I am downloading a GGUF version that has already been converted and often quantized for this runtime.
What is quantization again?
A model is mostly weights. Weights are numbers. For example:
If we store these numbers in high precision, the model needs more memory. For example, FP16 uses:
16 bits per weight
So a rough estimate for a 7B model is:

7 billion weights × 2 bytes
≈ 14 GB
That is just for weights. It does not include KV cache, activations, runtime overhead, or other memory usage. Quantization stores weights with fewer bits. For example:

FP16 → 16 bits
INT8 → 8 bits
INT4 → 4 bits
The rough memory idea becomes:

FP16 model → larger
Q8 model → smaller
Q4 model → much smaller
Why does quantization help local inference?
Because local machines and CPU servers may not have enough memory or bandwidth for large full-precision models. Quantization helps by:

reducing model size
reducing memory usage
improving cache efficiency
making models easier to load
making inference possible on smaller machines
For example, a model that is too large in FP16 may become practical in Q4. This is one of the main reasons local inference became more accessible.
Does quantization make the model worse?
Sometimes. Quantization is a tradeoff. We are storing approximate versions of the original weights. That can reduce quality. But the quality drop may be acceptable depending on:

model size
quantization level
task difficulty
prompt style
expected answer quality
For many tasks, a quantized model can still be useful. For harder reasoning, coding, long-context analysis, or high-accuracy tasks, the difference may become more visible. So again, the question is:
Is this model good enough for this task?
Not:
Is this model universally best?
How should I think about Q4, Q5, Q8, and F16?
A simple mental model:

F16
=
larger memory usage,
better precision

Q8
=
smaller than F16,
often still strong quality

Q4 / Q5
=
much smaller,
more practical for local inference,
possible quality tradeoff

This is not a universal rule for every model and every task. But it helps as a starting point. If I want maximum quality and have enough memory, I may try higher precision. If I want local speed and lower memory usage, I may try Q4 or Q5. If I want a middle ground, Q8 may be useful.
Why do GGUF filenames look confusing?
Because the filename often includes both the model name and quantization type. Example:
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf
This tells us:

Model family: Qwen2.5
Model size: 7B
Instruction-tuned: Instruct
Quantization: Q4_K_M
Format: GGUF
At first, these names look noisy. But once the pattern becomes clear, they are useful. They tell us what we are about to run.
What happens when llama.cpp runs a model?
At a high level:

Load GGUF model
Initialize runtime
Tokenize prompt
Run prefill
Create KV cache
Run decode loop
Generate tokens
Stream or return output
This should look familiar now. Even though we are using llama.cpp instead of vLLM, many inference concepts still apply:

tokens
prefill
decode
KV cache
batching
latency
tokens/sec
memory usage
That is important. The runtime is different, but the core inference behavior is still related.
Does llama.cpp also use KV cache?

Yes. Autoregressive generation still needs previous context. During prefill, the model processes the prompt and builds KV cache. During decode, new tokens are generated one at a time, and the KV cache grows. So even in local inference, the same mental model applies:

Prompt tokens fill the KV cache.
Generated tokens extend the KV cache.
Longer context uses more memory.
This is why context length matters even for CPU inference.
Why does context length matter?
Because the longer the context, the more KV cache memory is needed. A short prompt may be easy. A long document may be much harder. For example:
500 tokens
is very different from:
32,000 tokens

Even if the model weights fit, the KV cache can become a major memory consumer. This connects directly to the earlier inference articles. Model size is not the only memory problem. Runtime state matters too.
What is prefill like in llama.cpp?
Prefill is when the prompt is processed. If the prompt is long, prefill takes longer. That affects:
time to first token
So when I benchmark local inference, I should not only look at final generation speed. I should also measure:
How long until the first token appears?
A model may generate tokens quickly after it starts, but still have slow prefill for long prompts.
What is decode like in llama.cpp?
Decode is the token-by-token generation loop. This affects:

tokens per second
inter-token latency
streaming speed
If the decode speed is low, the response feels slow even after the first token appears. So for local inference, I want to measure both:

TTFT
and
tokens/sec
because they show different parts of the user experience.
Why does tokens/sec matter?
Tokens/sec tells us how quickly the model generates output. For example:
5 tokens/sec
feels very different from:
40 tokens/sec
For interactive chat, tokens/sec matters a lot. For batch processing, throughput may matter more than streaming feel. So again, the right metric depends on the workload.
Why does TTFT matter?
TTFT means:
Time To First Token
This is how long the user waits before seeing the first generated token. TTFT is affected by:

queueing
prompt length
prefill speed
runtime overhead
hardware speed
model size
For a chat application, TTFT strongly affects perceived responsiveness. Even if total generation is fast, a long pause before the first token can feel bad.
What should I benchmark first?
For my own learning, I would start simple:

same model
same prompt
different quantization
Example:

Qwen2.5 7B Q4_K_M
vs
Qwen2.5 7B Q8_0
Then compare:

memory usage
TTFT
tokens/sec
latency
answer quality
After that, change one more variable:

same model
same quantization
different CPU shape
Then compare again. The important rule is:
Change one variable at a time.
Otherwise, the benchmark becomes hard to understand.
What variables matter in CPU inference?
A few important ones are:

model size
quantization format
number of CPU cores
CPU generation
memory bandwidth
thread count
context length
prompt length
output length
batch size
runtime build options
This is why CPU inference experiments can be surprisingly interesting. There are many small knobs that affect performance.
Why does thread count matter?
llama.cpp can use CPU threads to parallelize work. But more threads are not always automatically better. At some point:

thread overhead
memory bandwidth limits
CPU topology
can affect scaling. So it is useful to benchmark different thread counts instead of assuming the highest number is always best. This is a very practical learning point.
Why does native build matter?

A portable build is safer because it can run across more machines. A native build can compile for the specific CPU features available on the machine. That may improve performance. But it may also introduce compatibility issues if certain instructions are not supported. This is exactly the kind of thing I want to learn from hands-on experiments. Conceptually, we can say:

portable build
=
more compatible

native build
=
potentially faster,
but more hardware-specific
How does this connect to my OCI inference workbench?
Wokbench: https://github.com/aruanurag/llm-inference-lab/tree/main/apps/oci-inference-cloud
This is where the topic becomes hands-on for me. I recently started building a small inference cloud workbench for my own learning. The idea is simple:

provision infrastructure
deploy llama.cpp
download a GGUF model
start an endpoint
run benchmarks
compare results
clean up infrastructure

This gives me a repeatable loop. Instead of manually setting up everything every time, I can create experiments and compare them. That matters because inference learning needs repetition. One benchmark is not enough. I want to compare:

different models
different quantization formats
different shapes
different CPU counts
different prompts
different workloads
Why start with CPU on OCI?
Because it is simpler and still useful. Before jumping into GPUs, I want to understand:

How far can CPU inference go?
What does performance look like?
Which small models are usable?
How does quantization affect latency?
How does model size affect memory?
What does routing to a CPU model feel like?
Starting with CPU also keeps the feedback loop smaller. It lets me focus on fundamentals:

model loading
endpoint serving
benchmarking
TTFT
tokens/sec
latency
cleanup
These concepts will still matter later when I move to GPU inference.
Does CPU inference replace GPU inference?

No. This is important. CPU inference is not replacing GPU inference. For large models, high concurrency, long context, and low-latency production serving, GPUs are still extremely important. The better mental model is:

CPU inference
=
useful for smaller models,
local workloads,
experiments,
edge use cases,
and cost-sensitive tasks

GPU inference
=
important for larger models,
higher throughput,
lower latency,
and production-scale serving
So the future is not:
CPU vs GPU
It is more like:
CPU + GPU + NPU + routing
where the system chooses the right destination for each workload.
How does this connect to model routing?
Once we have a CPU inference endpoint, we can start routing requests. For example:

Simple request
  ↓
small quantized model on CPU

Complex request
  ↓
larger model on GPU or hosted endpoint

This is a very practical architecture. Not every request needs the most expensive model. If a smaller CPU model can answer well enough, that may reduce cost and improve privacy. If the request is too hard, the router can escalate to a stronger model. So CPU inference becomes one destination in a broader model routing system.
What does the architecture look like?
A simple local experiment may look like:

User
  ↓
Local app
  ↓
Router
  ├── CPU model endpoint
  └── Hosted LLM endpoint
The CPU model endpoint may be backed by:

llama.cpp
+
GGUF model
+
quantized weights
This is a small version of a bigger production idea:

route each request to the cheapest model
that can still solve it well enough
Where does Ollama fit?
Ollama is often used as an easy local model running experience. It makes it simple to download and run models locally. A useful mental model:

llama.cpp
=
low-level local inference runtime

Ollama
=
developer-friendly local model experience

This is not a deep technical comparison. But for learning, it helps. If I want more direct control over flags, builds, models, and benchmarks, llama.cpp is very useful. If I want a smoother local user experience, Ollama is very convenient.
Where does GGUF fit in that ecosystem?

GGUF is the model format that makes these local inference workflows easier. A model in GGUF format can be distributed with quantization already applied. Then tools like llama.cpp can load it and run inference. So the flow often looks like:

Choose model
Choose GGUF quantization
Download file
Run with llama.cpp
Benchmark
Compare output
This is why GGUF appears so frequently in local inference discussions.
What is the biggest mental shift for me?
Earlier, I mostly thought about inference in terms of:
large GPU serving systems
Now I am starting to see a broader picture:

large GPU serving
+
local CPU inference
+
quantized models
+
routing
+
edge use cases
This makes inference feel more like a platform problem. The platform may include:

small local models
CPU endpoints
GPU endpoints
hosted APIs
routers
benchmarking
observability
cost controls
The model is only one part. The system around the model decides how useful and efficient it becomes.
What should we not overclaim?
It is easy to get excited about local inference and say:
Everything will run locally.

I do not think that is the right view. Local inference is powerful, but it has limits. Small models are improving, but large models still matter. CPU inference is useful, but GPUs still matter. Quantization helps, but it can affect quality. So the practical view is:

Use local inference where it fits.
Use larger GPU models where they are needed.
Use routing to decide between them.
What is the key mental model?
I would summarize this article like this:

llama.cpp
helps run LLMs efficiently
on local and CPU-friendly environments.

GGUF
packages models in a format
that works well with llama.cpp.

Quantization
reduces model size
so models can run on smaller hardware.

CPU inference
does not replace GPU inference,
but it expands where inference can run.
How does this connect back to the full inference stack?
The stack now looks something like:

Application
  ↓
Router
  ↓
Inference endpoint
  ↓
Runtime
  ↓
Hardware
For a llama.cpp CPU endpoint:

Application
  ↓
Router
  ↓
llama.cpp server
  ↓
GGUF model
  ↓
CPU
For a vLLM GPU endpoint:

Application
  ↓
Router
  ↓
vLLM replica
  ↓
GPU workers
  ↓
GPU
The outer architecture can be similar. But the runtime and hardware are different.
Why does this matter for LLMOps?
Because LLMOps is not only about deploying the biggest model. It is about:

choosing the right model
choosing the right hardware
measuring performance
controlling cost
monitoring latency
maintaining reliability
improving user experience
CPU inference gives one more option in that toolbox. And once model routing becomes part of the system, this becomes even more important.
What comes next?
Now that llama.cpp, GGUF, quantization, and CPU inference are clearer, the next natural step is hands-on. The next article should probably be:
Running CPU Inference Experiments on OCI
That would connect this concept article with actual experiments:

provisioning an instance
deploying llama.cpp
choosing a GGUF model
starting an endpoint
running benchmarks
measuring TTFT
measuring tokens/sec
comparing quantization formats
cleaning up infrastructure
That is the direction I am personally excited about now. The conceptual foundation has been useful. But the next phase should be much more practical. I want to see:

real latency numbers
real throughput numbers
real model behavior
real tradeoffs
Because at the end of the day, inference systems are learned best by running them.
